How we know, and where we stopone paragraph, the gate, and the boundary

How we know

Couro reconstructs the body in three dimensions from ordinary phone video. Joint angles from that reconstruction were compared against a marker-based motion-capture lab on the public OpenCap validation set (270 drop-jump trials, five camera angles): knee flexion agrees to within about 4 degrees, with hip and trunk in the same range. On real single-camera phone footage, 14 metric-and-view combinations reached Lin's concordance of 0.64 to 0.94 against lab motion capture.

The gate

Two captures are compared only when they share the same athlete, the same task, the same view and a similar framing. Anything else is kept, labelled with the reason, and never charted as change. The band on the drift chart is the range of this athlete's own compared captures, not a population norm. When the film is too occluded, too far or too dark to measure, the report says so and names the angle to film next time, rather than guessing.

Where we stop

Couro does not predict injury and does not diagnose. It measures how an athlete moves and flags change against that athlete's own baseline, in plain language, for a qualified person to read. The frontal-plane knee numbers on the scoreboard are shown as reported, as a review flag, and that measurement is one of the two we want to validate on Cal's equipment before anyone leans on it.
